newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead cut to 8.7 pct; Dole still in trouble.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead cut to 8.7 pct; Dole still in trouble.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's campaign lead over Republican Bob Dole narrowed to 8.7 percent in Thursday's Reuters tracking poll.

Clinton had the support of 45 percent of likely voters compared with the 36.3 percent who chose Dole. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot got 5.3 percent of the vote, 2.9 percent chose "other" and 10.5 percent were still undecided, with less than two weeks before the Nov. 5 Election Day.

The poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, reflects polling from Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.
Daily tracking polls can produce sharp fluctuations because of the relatively small size of the daily sample. Their main value is in plotting trends over a number of days.

"Bob Dole had a good day on Wednesday and that will happen in daily tracking," Zogby said in a telephone interview. "However, for Dole to have any chance of narrowing it further ... there are certain hurdles he has to be able to leap over."

Zogby said Dole must raise his support among Republicans which at present is less than 80 percent. Dole needs 90 percent of the Republican vote as well as strong support from those Americans who feel the country is on the "wrong track."
The tracking poll results on Thursday did not reflect Dole's plea for Perot to quit the presidential race and endorse Dole.

"Were Perot to drop out of the race, (Dole) would pick up two out of three of those Perot voters," Zogby said. "That could give him some momentum to build. But the reality check is, Dole needs a deus ex machina (divine intervention) and nothing less than that."
The presidential race remains close among voters over 50, but Clinton leads by better than two-to-one among younger Generation X voters and moderates.

Republicans hold a narrow lead in the race for control of Congress. The poll found 37.1 percent of those surveyed would vote for a Republican in their Congressional district compared with 36.1 percent for a Democrat.
